claims.headline: It speaks like an adult before it speaks like a child.
claims.text: At 12 months #1–#3 put 3.5 real words into an utterance; children in the same recordings put 0.9. The short, telegraphic speech of a two-year-old does not grow out of adult input alone.

dimensions.name: Grammar
dimensions.question: Which grammar does it learn, and what helps it learn more?

claims.headline: Word endings come early. Agreement stays shaky.
claims.text: Regular past tense passes at 12–15 months. Subject–verb agreement hovers near 70% for six years. Irregular past drops below chance at 8–12 months and recovers, without the earlier phase of correct, memorised forms that children show.

claims.headline: A bigger learner, or more of the right sentences, did not teach more grammar.
claims.text: A learner 2.4 times larger passed as many tests and memorised its input instead. Doubling one kind of sentence did no better than doubling random sentences. For two of the three phenomena the added sentences did not match what the test asks, so this is a weak test.

dimensions.name: Memory
dimensions.question: When the input changes later in life, what is kept and what is lost?

claims.headline: Books alone erase conversation. Three parts in ten of talk keep it.
claims.text: Six months of books only made held-out adult speech as hard as at a much younger age. Clones that heard the same books with 30% conversation kept it and learnt the books just as well.

dimensions.name: Inheritance
dimensions.question: When one generation teaches the next, what is passed on and what changes?

claims.headline: Children inherit the slips of the copy they heard.
claims.text: Children raised on #1's copy and on #2's copy each said more of their own parent's new word pairs (cross ratio 2.51, 95% interval 1.70–3.80). The more often a slip appeared in the copy, the more the children used it.

dimensions.name: Lesions
dimensions.question: When an adult is damaged, what goes first?
